Childbirth analgesia

One 29-person randomized study reported a reduction in pain after red and near-infrared LED exposure during labor, with similar fetal, newborn, and labor-duration measures between groups. Postpartum perineal studies are mixed, and recent reviews found no clear average added benefit.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One 29-person randomized study reported a reduction in pain after red and near-infrared LED exposure during labor, with similar fetal, newborn, and labor-duration measures between groups. Postpartum perineal studies are mixed, and recent reviews found no clear average added benefit.

Summary of the Evidence

Eleven records are relevant to light-based analgesia around childbirth. Nine are filed under Childbirth: five randomized publications, one observational cohort, and three meta-analyses that overlap the original studies. Two narrowly mapped records add a labor-specific trial protocol and a randomized trial filed under perineal trauma. Only one completed study directly tested pain during labor; the other empirical reports address postpartum perineal injuries and should be interpreted separately.

Human and clinical evidence

The intrapartum randomized study compared a single LED-plate exposure with a hot shower in 29 women. It reported a statistically significant reduction in pain ratings after LED treatment. The abstract reports no between-group differences in fetal well-being, Apgar scores, or labor duration, but does not give a clear between-group estimate for pain. It therefore documents an immediate decrease after exposure without firmly establishing that the plate outperformed the comparator (Traverzim et al. 2021).

Postpartum findings are mixed. A randomized 56-person comparison found a greater pain reduction with PBM than cryotherapy immediately after delivery and at 24 hours. In contrast, a 59-person double-blind sham-controlled trial found no clinical improvement in pain or healing after a single 660-nm application, and another small sham-controlled trial reported no acceleration of episiotomy healing (Santos et al. 2012). A 2025 randomized trial filed under perineal trauma also found no advantage over sham after one application. Recent systematic reviews pooled postpartum studies and found no clear average benefit for pain or healing, with substantial variation among trials (Constant et al. 2024; de Castro et al. 2026; Gondim et al. 2025; Alayat et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly examining PBM for childbirth analgesia was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No direct cell-culture or ex-vivo evidence was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The labor study used one 10-minute exposure from a plate combining 660-nm red visible light and 850-nm near-infrared light over the back from T10 to S4. Postpartum protocols used different laser or LED devices, anatomical sites, doses, and schedules. For example, one sham-controlled perineal trial used 780-nm near-infrared light over three days, while the recent null trial used 660-nm red light at 4 J. A dorsal labor treatment cannot be assumed to act like local perineal treatment.

Interpretation

The single intrapartum study reported an immediate pain reduction, but its small size and unclear between-group pain estimate leave the comparative effect uncertain. Postpartum perineal results vary, and pooled reviews have not shown a clear average improvement. These are distinct clinical questions and should not be combined into one estimate.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for short-term pain reduction during labor Low for added pain or healing benefit after postpartum perineal injury
Publications and records11 relevant records, including 9 in Childbirth and 2 narrowly mapped

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Only one 29-person randomized study examined pain during labor, and its report does not clearly establish a between-group advantage. Postpartum perineal studies are a separate setting; recent pooled reviews found no clear average improvement over controls, despite favorable individual trials. Replicated intrapartum trials and larger postpartum studies with common pain and healing outcomes are needed.
